form: Phyllis spent a lot of her childhood living a traditional lifestyle on the land, helping her parents and grandparents with fishing, gathering firewood, picking berries, and digging shellfish. Her father had a houseboat he would tow behind his boat when he went fishing and logging, so the family could stay together, travelling up and down the coast. Her parents used to hide her and her older brother in the fishbox on the boat to avoid the priest and policeman when they came looking for kids to send to residential school. Finally, though, when she was 10, she was taken to residential school in Sechelt. There, though she was beaten for using her language, she was determined to maintain it and would hide, speaking it with her friends. At 14, she left residential school because she became ill. She was taken to Saint Paul’s hospital, where she found another little boy who also spoke ʔayʔaǰuθəm, and they would speak together.
gloss: the second paragraph of §1. Saint Paul’s hospital is the St. Paul’s Hospital of §4

form: In her adult life, Phyllis lived many years in Seattle, before moving back to Tla’amin, and later to Vancouver. In Seattle, she spoke with relatives in the language, and later when living in Vancouver, she would keep in touch with other ʔayʔaǰuθəm speakers on the phone. It was during her time living in Vancouver that she started to work regularly with linguists and welcomed this additional opportunity to use her language and contribute to the documentary record available to future generations. We loved working with her. She took the language work very seriously and yet always had a chuckle and had fun with it. On each visit, we were welcomed into her house with great generosity, as if we were members of her own family.

form: In the following narrative, Phyllis recounts how she and her brother got taken to residential school in Sechelt, and how her grandfather encouraged them not to forget their language. Despite the severe mistreatment by the priests and nuns, she managed to remember her language. The story was recorded on May 27, 2018 by Kaining Xu in St. Paul’s Hospital, Vancouver, BC. Phyllis was recovering from pneumonia in the hospital, but eager to continue working in the language. She dreamed about her grandparents the night before, and hand-wrote five stories in English. This story is one of them. Kaining encouraged her to tell this story in ʔayʔaǰuθəm. The written version was only a starting point, however, and Phyllis’s oral version in ʔayʔaǰuθəm is quite different from the written version. We include the handwritten story in Section 4.1, typed to represent the writing faithfully, to help situate the story we present here and provide additional history and context.
